questions.question: Q: What is active citizenship and why is it important?

points.text: Active citizenship means taking part in community and political life to improve society. It is important because it strengthens democracy, holds those in power to account, addresses social issues directly, and empowers individuals and communities to make a difference.

questions.question: Q: Give three examples of active citizenship.

points.text: 1) Volunteering at a food bank to help people experiencing poverty. 2) Campaigning for better recycling facilities by organising a petition and meeting the local council. 3) Voting in elections and encouraging others to do the same through a voter registration drive.

questions.question: Q: What are the barriers to active citizenship?

points.text: Barriers include lack of time (especially for people in low-paid work), lack of confidence or knowledge about how to participate, lack of financial resources, language barriers for non-native speakers, and a sense that participation will not make a difference (political disengagement).

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Active citizenship is essential for a healthy democracy because it ensures power remains in the hands of the people. When citizens participate — by voting, campaigning, or holding representatives to account — they ensure government reflects the will of the people. Without participation, democracy becomes symbolic rather than real. Active citizenship provides a check on power. Investigative journalism, pressure groups, and public protests expose government failures and demand accountability. The Windrush scandal was exposed through active citizenship by campaigners and journalists. Furthermore, active citizenship addresses issues that government alone cannot solve. Food banks, youth clubs, and environmental clean-ups are often run by volunteers who fill gaps in public services. This strengthens communities and builds social cohesion. However, barriers to participation mean not all citizens can be equally active, meaning democracy may disproportionately reflect the voices of more privileged citizens.
